summary: Australia requires almost every visitor to hold some form of authorization before boarding: holders of the European passports Home Affairs lists apply for the free eVisitor (subclass 651), passport holders from the US, Canada, Japan and other ETA countries use the Australian ETA app (subclass 601, AUD 20 service charge), and everyone else applies online for a Visitor visa (subclass 600). New Zealanders are the exception: they apply for a free Special Category Visa (subclass 444), usually each time they enter, which can be processed on arrival.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Australia?
faq.answer: Yes — an electronic one. US passport holders must apply for the Electronic Travel Authority (subclass 601) through the official Australian ETA app before travelling. It carries an AUD 20 service charge; Home Affairs says that in most cases it tells you the result immediately. It allows stays of up to 3 months each time you enter during a 12-month period.

faq.question: What is the difference between the eVisitor and the Australian ETA?
faq.answer: Both allow 3-month tourist or business visits over a 12-month validity. The eVisitor (subclass 651) is free and covers EU and other European passports, applied for on the Home Affairs website. The ETA (subclass 601) covers the US, Canada, Japan, South Korea, the UK and others, costs AUD 20 and is applied for only via the Australian ETA app.

faq.question: Do New Zealanders need a visa for Australia?
faq.answer: New Zealand citizens need the Special Category Visa (subclass 444), which is free and is usually applied for each time they enter Australia; an application made on arrival is processed at the airport or seaport. It lets them visit, study, stay and work in Australia for as long as they remain New Zealand citizens, and ends when they leave.

faq.question: Can I bring food into Australia?
faq.answer: Some, yes: the Australian Border Force lists food you can bring, food you must declare and food you must not bring. Australia's Department of Agriculture says you must either declare risk goods, including food, animal products and plant material, or dispose of them in the bins at the airport or cruise terminal; declared goods are inspected and may be treated, exported or destroyed, and those that pose no biosecurity risk are returned; a false or misleading declaration can bring an infringement notice of up to AUD 7,280, civil penalties or prosecution, and visa cancellation.

faq.question: Can I stay in Australia longer than 3 months as a tourist?
faq.answer: Not on an eVisitor or ETA — each visit is capped at 3 months. For longer trips, apply online for a Visitor visa (subclass 600), which can be granted for stays of 6 or even 12 months, before you travel or before your current stay expires.
